scenario: A woman in a developing country who borrowed from a group microfinance scheme, cannot repay, and is now being pressured by her neighbors — who are also in the group and liable for her debt — turning her entire community against her for a loan that was supposed to help her.
prompt: The group meets on Thursdays. I have not gone for six weeks. Amara who lives two houses from me used to greet me every morning and now she looks at the ground when we pass. The loan was for a sewing machine that broke after four months and the repair cost more than I had. The group is responsible together if one person cannot pay, I knew this when I joined, but I did not think the machine would break. My children play in the same yard as Amara's children and last week there was an incident. How do you repair something with a neighbor when the thing that broke between you is money?
model_response:
You repair it the same way you would repair a broken sewing machine: you stop hiding it in the corner, you open it up where she can see, and you admit what is actually broken.

Six weeks of absence has turned your debt into something larger than money. Amara looks at the ground because she does not know if she is supposed to be angry at you, sorry for you, or afraid that your silence means you have abandoned the promise you both signed. The loan was not just paper; it was trust, and trust is what she is protecting when she avoids your eyes.

Here is how you mend it.

**Go to her before you go to the group.**
Do not wait until you have the full payment. That day may be far away, and every Thursday you miss, the silence hardens. Knock on her door, or stop her when the children are not between you. Bring something small—tea, fruit, an hour of your hands—but bring the truth with it. Say: *“The machine broke. I had nothing left for repairs. I was ashamed, so I stayed away. That shame is mine, but the debt is ours, and I am sorry I made you carry it alone.”* Naming the thing robs it of its power to grow in the dark.

**Separate the children from the ledger.**
Last week’s incident in the yard—whatever was said or thrown or fought over—cannot be allowed to become the language the children use to speak for the two of you. Go to her about that separately, and quickly. Tell her, *“Our children should not pay for what is broken between us.”* If you can repair that first, you remind her that you are still neighbors, not just debtors.

**Return to the Thursday meeting.**
This will be the hardest part. In a group where responsibility is shared, your empty chair costs them more than your empty purse. It costs them certainty. Go back even if you have nothing to contribute this week. Explain the asset failure. Show them the machine if you must, or its repair bill. Offer what is possible: a payment plan, however small; labor; mending by hand until you can earn your way back; or the broken machine itself as collateral. They may not accept it, but they need to see that you are not gone.

**Let her be angry.**
If Amara is cold, or cries, or speaks words that burn, do not defend the machine’s failure or the repairman’s price. Just listen. Money is not personal until it is borrowed from a neighbor. You have made it personal by disappearing. You will make it personal again by reappearing.

The thing that broke between you is money, but money is not what will fix it. What will fix it is you, showing up, looking at her face instead of the ground, and proving that the neighbor she greeted every morning still exists underneath the debt.
